Guide.title: Pool Maintenance Guide
Guide.subtitle: Everything you need to keep your water clear, balanced and safe.

chemistry.title: Chemistry
chemistry.intro: Three parameters keep the water balanced: alkalinity (80-120 ppm), pH (7.2-7.6) and free chlorine (1-3 ppm). Always check them in this order — alkalinity, pH, chlorine — because each one affects the next.

alkalinity.title: Alkalinity
alkalinity.p1: Alkalinity acts as a buffer for pH: it cushions the sudden swings you'd otherwise get when adding a product, which is why you fix it before the pH. But buffered doesn't mean frozen — a high alkalinity actively pushes pH upward. The higher the alkalinity, the more dissolved carbon dioxide the water tends to release into the air, and every time that happens the pH rises. In practice: with high alkalinity the pH climbs back quickly and you need acid constantly, while bringing it toward the low end of the range slows that climb and settles the pH lower.
alkalinity.p2: In a pool, alkalinity tends to decrease over time because acidic products such as pH reducer consume the bicarbonates in the water. To bring it back into range, use sodium bicarbonate — which also slightly raises the pH.

ph.title: pH
ph.p1: pH measures the acidity of the water. A value between 7.2 and 7.6 lets every other product (chlorine, algaecide, flocculant, clarifier) work at peak efficiency. Tap water is slightly basic (pH ≈ 7.5).
ph.p2: In a pool, pH tends to rise over time due to rain and exposure to air. To lower it, the usual choice in Italy is the pool pH reducer sold in granules or liquid form. English-language guides often recommend muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid) instead: it works, and much of the source material cited on this site is based on it, but it is not the common choice here and it is considerably more aggressive to handle. To raise pH, use sodium carbonate — though it also nudges alkalinity upward.

chlorine.title: Chlorine
chlorine.p1: Chlorine disinfects the water, preventing algae and dangerous bacteria. It comes in several forms — tablets, granules, liquid — each with a different concentration and level of stabilization.

chlorineStabilized.title: Stabilized chlorine
chlorineStabilized.p1: Trichlor tablets (typically 200 g) and 56% dichlor isocyanurate granules are both stabilized chlorines: they contain cyanuric acid that shields them from sunlight. Dichlor is very strong and acts quickly.

chlorineUnstabilized.title: Unstabilized chlorine
chlorineUnstabilized.p1: Sodium hypochlorite is a liquid chlorine at 12-15% active chlorine, with no stabilizer, used for shocks. Calcium hypochlorite is a granular form at 70-73% active chlorine, also unstabilized and suitable for shocks. The two differ in physical state (liquid/solid), concentration (~15% vs. ~73%) and pH (13 vs. 11).
chlorineUnstabilized.p2: For the same shock, calcium hypochlorite needs roughly one-fifth the weight compared to sodium. Both temporarily raise pH by about one point, because hypochlorite breaks down into hydrochloric acid (HCl) and a base; once the reaction is complete the pH returns almost to its starting point, so the net pH change after a shock is negligible.
chlorineUnstabilized.p3: ⚠️ Never mix hypochlorite with other types of chlorine: risk of explosion, fire and toxic fumes.

chloramines.title: Chloramines
chloramines.p1: When chlorine reacts with organic matter it forms chloramines (combined chlorine), which disinfect far less effectively than free chlorine. The most effective way to keep them low is simply to add more chlorine.

stabilizer.title: Stabilizer
stabilizer.p1: The stabilizer is cyanuric acid, present in trichlor tablets and in dichlor isocyanurate. It protects chlorine from UV destruction. The ideal range is 30-50 ppm: below 30 chlorine degrades too quickly in sunlight; above 50 chlorine becomes "bound" and loses effectiveness.
stabilizer.p2: Warning: repeatedly using dichlor isocyanurate for shocks rapidly raises the stabilizer level. Once it is too high, the only way to lower it is a partial drain of the pool.

hardness.title: Hardness
hardness.p1: Calcium hardness must sit between 175 and 400 ppm. Below that, water tends to corrode concrete; above it, scale forms on pipes and liner. Well-balanced hardness, together with alkalinity, helps keep pH stable.
hardness.p2: If hardness is too high, it can be treated with a sequestering agent.

algaecide.title: Algaecide
algaecide.p1: Algaecide is a preventive product that stops algae from taking hold. Specific formulations also exist for removing algae once they have appeared.

flocculant.title: Flocculant
flocculant.p1: Flocculant binds suspended particles, making them heavy enough to settle on the bottom. It is especially useful after a shock that killed off a lot of dark-green algae, when the water stays cloudy.

cleaning.title: Cleaning
cleaning.intro: The first line of defense against algae and cloudy water is constantly removing debris. The less organic food there is in the water, the less work the chlorine has to do.

circulation.title: Circulation
circulation.p1: Good water circulation is essential: the hotter it gets, the more hours the pump should run. As a general rule, 12 hours a day is a safe baseline, but the exact number depends on the pool volume and the pump's flow rate (usually expressed in gallons per hour).
circulation.p2: Temperature matters a lot: in summer you typically need roughly twice the hours compared to winter.

debris.title: Debris
debris.p1: You have to constantly remove organic and inorganic debris from the water. Organic debris (leaves, insects, pollen) feeds algae; inorganic debris (sand, dust) clouds the water. A fine-mesh skimmer net, used daily, is the first line of routine maintenance.

robot.title: Cleaning robot
robot.p1: The cleaning robot has a filter of just a few microns: it is perfect for vacuuming fine algae and particles off the bottom. For routine use, it is the most convenient way to keep the floor spotless without any manual work.

actions.title: Actions
actions.intro: Beyond day-to-day maintenance, a pool needs scheduled periodic interventions: shocks to restore the disinfectant, filter cleaning and floor cleaning.

shock.title: Shock
shock.p1: A shock consists of dumping a large amount of chlorine into the water to sterilize it and wipe out every organism. For it to work, alkalinity and pH must be in the correct range. Brushing every surface is equally important: putting algae into suspension exposes them to the chlorine.
shock.p2: In normal conditions free chlorine sits between 1 and 3 ppm; in a shock you aim for 10 ppm, and up to 30 ppm in severe cases. Calcium hypochlorite is the best choice because just a few kilograms produce a powerful shock; sodium hypochlorite also works well.
shock.p3: A shock is typically done about once a week (often less). Strong sun, heat and a heavy bather load are the factors that make it most necessary.

filterCleaning.title: Filter cleaning
filterCleaning.p1: The sand filter catches suspended particles. In normal conditions, cleaning it every 1-2 weeks is enough. After a shock, on the other hand, it should be cleaned immediately and more thoroughly — especially if the water was overrun with algae.

bottomCleaning.title: Bottom cleaning
bottomCleaning.p1: Routine floor cleaning is done with the robot. When large amounts of algae have settled on the bottom, switch to the manual vacuum with the selector set to waste, to drain the debris straight outside instead of pushing it through the filter.

formulas.description: The three chlorine quantities are tied together: if you know two of them, the third one follows.

Info.title: How the comparison works
Info.subtitle: Why the sticker price alone isn't enough.

overview.title: Overview
overview.p1: This tool doesn't compare the sticker price of the two packages — it compares the real cost per kilogram of active chlorine, the disinfecting ingredient actually contained in the product. That's the only correct way to tell which product is really the better deal.

slots.title: Two free slots, not two fixed chemicals
slots.p1: Each side of the comparison is an independent slot, Product A and Product B, and you pick the chemical inside it. That means you can compare two different products (a calcium hypochlorite against a sodium hypochlorite) or two products of the same type — two sodium hypochlorites from different shops, for instance, which is the everyday question when you're standing in front of a shelf.
slots.p2: The winner is announced as "Product A" or "Product B", never as a chemical name: if both slots hold the same chemical, naming the chemical would tell you nothing about which package to buy.

activeChlorine.title: Why count "active chlorine"
activeChlorine.p1: Two products at the same package price can have very different chlorine concentrations: a cheaper product per kilogram can end up costing more for the same amount of disinfection if its concentration is lower. That's why both products are converted to the same unit — cost per kilogram of active chlorine.
activeChlorine.formula: cost / active kg = total price ÷ active chlorine mass

table.title: The products you can compare
table.p1: Four products, and they are not interchangeable. The strengths are typical retail values used to prefill the fields — always read your own label, because the same product is sold at different concentrations.
table.p2: The last column is the one people miss. Two of these products carry cyanuric acid (the stabilizer) into the water with every dose, and that changes what "cheap" means.

solid.title: Solid products (sold by weight)
solid.p1: A solid is sold by weight, so the package weight is all that's needed — the active chlorine mass is the concentration percentage applied to the gross weight. Litres aren't offered for a solid, because a granular product has no meaningful volume price.

liquid.title: Liquid products (sold by volume or weight)
liquid.p1: A liquid can be sold by volume or by weight, so you choose the unit. If you enter litres, it's converted to weight using the product's density (shown on the label) — if you don't know it, a typical density of {density} kg/L for sodium hypochlorite solutions is used.

stabilized.title: Stabilized products: the price you don't see
stabilized.p1: Trichlor and dichlor contain chlorine and cyanuric acid together. They are the most concentrated products on the shelf, so on cost per kilogram of active chlorine they will often win this comparison outright. That verdict is true, and it is only half the story.
stabilized.p2: Trichlor brings {trichlor} ppm of stabilizer for every ppm of chlorine it delivers, dichlor {dichlor} ppm. The stabilizer stays in the water: it isn't consumed like chlorine and evaporation doesn't remove it. Past roughly {idealMax} ppm you need progressively more chlorine to get the same disinfection, and past {cyaHigh} ppm the standard advice is to dilute the pool with fresh water — the only practical way to bring it back down.
stabilized.p3: This is not a reason to never use them: they are convenient, and occasional use is fine. It's a reason to know what your stabilizer level is before making them a habit. This is also why the shock calculator doesn't offer them at all — a shock dose of stabilized chlorine delivers tens of ppm of cyanuric acid in a single afternoon.

verdict.title: How the winner is decided
verdict.p1: The slot with the lower cost per kilogram of active chlorine wins. The savings shown is the difference between the two active-kg costs — it tells you how much you're saving (or losing) for every kilogram of usable chlorine you buy.
verdict.p2: The verdict compares price only. If one of the two slots holds a stabilized product, read it together with the warning shown on that card: the cheaper product per kilogram can still be the more expensive choice for the pool.

limits.title: Assumptions & limits
limits.p1: Enter the price including VAT if applicable, otherwise the comparison isn't accurate. Use the concentration shown on the label at the time of purchase — liquid sodium hypochlorite degrades over time (heat, light, package age), so an old or poorly stored product may contain less active chlorine than stated. This tool doesn't model that decay, so on non-fresh product the real cost could be higher than calculated.

Info.title: How the Shock Calculator works
Info.subtitle: The full logic and formulas behind the result — nothing hidden.

overview.title: What this tool computes
overview.p1: It answers one question: how much chlorine product to pour in to bring your water to a safe shock level — given the pool volume, the water condition, the stabilizer (CYA) and the chlorine already present. Every step below is exactly what runs under the hood.

chlorine.title: Free, combined and total chlorine
chlorine.p1: Free chlorine (FC) is the active disinfectant. Combined chlorine (CC) is chlorine already bonded to organic matter — the weak, smelly 'used-up' chlorine (chloramines). Total chlorine (TC) is just FC + CC.
chlorine.p2: A shock works on FC: you push it well above normal to kill algae and burn off chloramines. So the dose depends on how far your current FC is from the target, and — when you provide it — on your CC.

target.title: Step 1 — The target free chlorine (SLAM)
target.p1: The target is not a fixed number: it scales with your cyanuric acid (CYA). CYA locks most of the chlorine into a reserve, leaving only a small fraction as active hypochlorous acid (HOCl). More CYA means less active chlorine at the same FC, so you need a higher FC. The TroubleFreePool 'SLAM' method captures this with a single ratio:
target.p2: That {pct} of CYA is the shock level that restores enough active HOCl no matter how much stabilizer is in the water.

whySlam.title: Why SLAM, and not a fixed dose
whySlam.p1: Two simpler approaches exist. A fixed target (e.g. '10 ppm, 30 in bad cases') is easy but ignores CYA, so it under-doses high-CYA pools — the chlorine is there but inactive — and over-doses low-CYA ones. The retail 'pounds per 10,000 gallons' rule is practical but tied to one product and one assumed CYA.
whySlam.p2: SLAM is the only model where what matters is the FC-to-CYA ratio, not absolute FC. '10 ppm' is meaningless without knowing CYA. By anchoring on {pct} of CYA, the same killing power is reached whether your CYA is 30 or 90 — that is why this tool uses it, and why it asks for your CYA (or a prudent estimate when you don't know it).
whySlam.p3: We stay honest about the limit: above {cyaHigh} ppm of CYA, even shock-level FC struggles, and the real fix is partly draining and refilling. The tool warns you instead of demanding an impossible dose.

breakpoint.title: Step 1b — Breakpoint (when combined chlorine is high)
breakpoint.p1: Destroying chloramines needs a separate push: FC has to cross a 'breakpoint' of about {mult} times the CC. Below it you create more chloramines; above it they break down into harmless nitrogen gas.
breakpoint.p2: The tool computes both targets and keeps the higher one, so a high CC raises your result on its own:
breakpoint.formula2: Final target = max( SLAM target , {mult} × CC , color minimum )
breakpoint.p3: Example: a SLAM target of 20 ppm with a CC of 3 ppm gives a breakpoint of 30 ppm, which wins — and the result tells you which one drove the number. The {mult}× rule is a conservative industry rule of thumb (some chemists argue the true demand is lower), so we label it as such.

color.title: Step 1c — How the water color changes the result
color.p1: The water condition sets a severity multiplier on the SLAM target, plus a minimum floor so a visible bloom is never under-treated:
color.p2: So at the same CYA, going from light green to very dark water multiplies the target — and therefore the product — by up to {maxMult}×. 'Perfect' water means no algae shock at all: the tool only suggests a breakpoint shock if your CC is above {ccHigh} ppm.

dose.title: Step 2 — From target to grams of pure chlorine
dose.p1: Once the target is known, the dose is simply the gap to fill across the whole pool. Since 1 ppm = 1 milligram per litre, one gram of pure chlorine raises 1,000 litres by 1 ppm:
dose.p2: If your current FC already meets the target, nothing needs to be added.

product.title: Step 3 — From pure chlorine to product
product.p1: You don't buy 'pure chlorine' — you buy a product at some strength, so we divide by its available-chlorine fraction. Stabilized chlorine (trichlor tablets, dichlor granules) is deliberately excluded: it adds CYA every single time, which is exactly what makes a pool unmanageable over a season.
product.p2: Liquid chlorine is sold in 'trade %' (grams of available chlorine per 100 mL); storing it internally as grams per litre avoids the classic weight-vs-volume dosing error. Each product also nudges the water:

unknowns.title: When you answer “I don't know”
unknowns.p1: If you don't know your CYA, the tool evaluates the target across a prudent range ({cyaMin}–{cyaMax} ppm). If you don't know your current chlorine, it spans {fcMin}–{fcMax} ppm. The headline figure is the average of that range, and a warning shows the full span — because without measuring, the honest answer is a range, not a single number.

safety.title: Assumptions & safety
safety.p1: Balance the pH first — a shock with bad pH wastes product. Never mix different chlorine products (toxic gas). Brush the surfaces to suspend algae. Re-test after the water has circulated, and wait until FC drops back to the normal band before swimming. These numbers are guidance, not a lab measurement.

Info.title: How the volume calculation works
Info.subtitle: The formula behind your pool's liters.

overview.title: Overview
overview.p1: The volume calculated here is used by the other tools (like the Shock Calculator) to dose chemical products correctly — the more accurate the estimate, the more reliable the suggested doses.

rectangle.title: Rectangular pool
rectangle.p1: The volume is the product of the three dimensions.

circle.title: Round pool
circle.p1: The volume is that of a cylinder: the area of the base circle multiplied by the depth.

depth.title: Why "average depth"
depth.p1: If the pool floor isn't flat (for example it slopes toward a deeper end), use the average between the shallowest and deepest points, not the maximum depth — using the deepest point would overestimate the real volume.

units.title: Units
units.p1: You can enter dimensions in meters or feet — the result is always shown in liters, cubic meters and US gallons, for compatibility with the English-language sources cited in the other tools.
units.formula: 1 foot = {meters} m · 1 m³ = 1000 L · 1 US gallon = {gal} L

limits.title: Limits
limits.p1: This tool only supports rectangular and round shapes. For freeform or irregular pools, the simplest estimate is to treat it as the smallest rectangle that contains it and adjust the result down, or ask a professional for an accurate measurement.

ChlorineMaintenance.title: Chlorine Maintenance
ChlorineMaintenance.description: How much chlorine to keep every day, and what your product is doing to your stabilizer.
ChlorineMaintenance.saltWaterNote: These figures are for pools chlorinated by hand (tablets, granules, liquid). Salt-water pools with a chlorine generator work to a different stabilizer range and are outside the scope of this tool.

volume.title: How much water is in the pool?
volume.subtitle: If you already worked this out in another tool, it's filled in for you.

cya.title: What is your stabilizer (CYA) level?
cya.subtitle: This single number decides how much chlorine your pool needs.
cya.unknownNote: No problem. You'll get a range instead of one number, calculated across the levels a typical pool sits at. The stabilizer projection needs a measured value though, so it stays off until you have one.

product.title: Which product do you use day to day?
product.subtitle: Not what you shock with, what you dose routinely.

fc.title: How much free chlorine is in there now?
fc.subtitle: So the tool can tell you what to add today.
fc.unknownNote: Fine. The dose is worked out for a range of plausible starting points, so treat it as a guide and test when you can.

demand.title: How much chlorine does the pool use per day?
demand.subtitle: This drives the stabilizer projection.
demand.howTo: Typical summer pools use {min} to {max} ppm a day, and you can measure yours: test free chlorine, add nothing for 24 hours, test again. The difference is your real daily demand, which beats any average.

Result.prompt: Fill in the pool volume and your stabilizer level to see your target.
Result.neverBelow: Never let it drop below {min} ppm, that's where algae starts winning.
Result.floorNote: At your stabilizer level the ratio alone would ask for less than this, but a lower target is impractical to test and hold, so the floor applies.
Result.atTarget: Your chlorine is already at target. Add nothing today.
Result.doseAddsCya: Careful: this dose also adds {cya} ppm of stabilizer.

Warnings.CYA_LOCK_RISK: You are still dosing a stabilized product into a pool whose stabilizer is already too high. Every dose makes the problem worse. Switch to an unstabilized chlorine (liquid or calcium hypochlorite) until the level comes down.
Warnings.CYA_HIGH: Your stabilizer is at or above {cyaHigh} ppm. At this level chlorine struggles whatever you do, and the standard advice is to replace part of the water with fresh, because nothing else lowers it.
Warnings.CYA_ABOVE_IDEAL: Your stabilizer is above the ideal ceiling of {idealMax} ppm. Nothing is broken yet, but from here you need more and more chlorine for the same result, and it only goes down by diluting.
Warnings.CYA_UNKNOWN_ASSUMED: These numbers assume a stabilizer level, because you don't know yours. Test it: it is the single measurement that decides everything else on this page.
Warnings.LOW_DOSE: The amount is so small it's hard to measure accurately. Consider dosing for two or three days at once instead.

Projection.title: Where your stabilizer is heading
Projection.needsCya: This projection needs a measured stabilizer level to start from. Guessing the starting point would turn an estimate into a countdown, which would be worse than saying nothing.

trend.rising: Your stabilizer is climbing, because the product you use carries it in with every dose.
trend.stable: Your stabilizer is holding steady: what the product adds and what sunlight destroys cancel out.
trend.falling: Your stabilizer is slowly falling. The product you use adds none, and sunlight destroys a little each month.

Projection.weeksToCeiling: At this rate you cross {ceiling} ppm in about {weeks} weeks.
Projection.noCeiling: At this rate you are not heading out of range, so there is no date to give you.
Projection.breakdownAdded: the product adds {added} ppm per week
Projection.breakdownDegraded: sunlight destroys {degraded} ppm per week ({monthly} ppm/month)
Projection.assumption: A straight-line estimate based on the daily chlorine demand you entered. It ignores the fact that a higher stabilizer level slowly reduces daily chlorine loss, so treat it as a direction, not a date in the diary.

Info.title: How the maintenance numbers work
Info.subtitle: Why there is no single right chlorine level.

overview.title: Overview
overview.p1: There is no universal correct amount of chlorine. The right level depends entirely on your stabilizer (cyanuric acid), because the stabilizer holds chlorine in reserve and keeps most of it inactive at any moment. The more stabilizer you have, the more total chlorine you need to end up with the same working amount.
overview.p2: This tool answers the daily question. The shock calculator answers a different one: how far to push chlorine once, to recover a pool that has already gone wrong.

ratio.title: The two numbers
ratio.p1: TroubleFreePool publishes the whole chlorine ladder as percentages of the stabilizer level. This tool uses two of them: the minimum you must not go below, and the target you should aim for so that a hot day or a busy weekend doesn't push you under it.
ratio.formulaMin: minimum chlorine = {pct} of stabilizer, and never below {floor} ppm
ratio.p2: The {floor} ppm floor matters at low stabilizer levels, where the percentage alone would ask for an amount too small to test or hold reliably. The published table stops following the percentage down at the same point.

classicRule.title: Why "1 to 3 ppm" is wrong
classicRule.p1: Almost every shop and leaflet gives a fixed range of 1 to 3 ppm of free chlorine. That advice ignores the stabilizer entirely, and it is the single most common reason a pool goes green while its test kit still shows chlorine.
classicRule.p2: It happens to be roughly right for a pool at the low end of the ideal stabilizer range, and it becomes dangerously low as the stabilizer climbs: at {cyaHigh} ppm of stabilizer the real minimum is {pct} of that, well over double the top of the classic advice. The number on your test strip has not changed. What that number means has.

lock.title: "Chlorine lock": a misleading name for a real problem
lock.p1: You will hear that too much stabilizer "locks" your chlorine, trapping it so it cannot work. Taken literally that is a myth, and it is worth knowing why, because the myth leads people to the wrong fix.
lock.p2: Chlorine and stabilizer sit in a continuous, reversible balance. The stabilizer acts as a reservoir: it keeps most of the chlorine parked and releases it as the active form gets used up. Nothing is trapped. What changes is the proportion: the more stabilizer in the water, the smaller the share of your chlorine that is active at any instant. Your test kit still reports the total, so the reading looks healthy while the pool is effectively under-chlorinated.
lock.p3: This is also different from "chlorine demand", where algae and organic matter eat chlorine as fast as you add it. The two get the same nickname and have opposite cures: over-stabilization is fixed by diluting the water, chlorine demand by adding more chlorine. Getting them the wrong way round wastes a season.

stabilized.title: Stabilized products: convenient, and cumulative
stabilized.p1: Trichlor tablets and dichlor granules contain chlorine and stabilizer together. Every ppm of chlorine from trichlor brings {trichlor} ppm of stabilizer with it; from dichlor, {dichlor} ppm. That is not a defect, it is what they are for: the stabilizer protects the chlorine from sunlight.
stabilized.p2: The catch is that the chlorine gets used up and the stabilizer does not. It accumulates. The ideal band is {idealMin} to {idealMax} ppm; past {cyaHigh} ppm the standard advice is to replace part of the water, because diluting is the only practical way to bring it down.
stabilized.p3: So they are fine to use, and worth keeping an eye on. What catches people out is not one dose, it is a habit repeated across a season without ever measuring the stabilizer. That is exactly what this tool is here to make visible.

projection.title: The projection, and what it assumes
projection.p1: If your product carries stabilizer, the projection follows it week by week. It is a balance of two things: what the product adds, and what sunlight destroys.
projection.formula: weekly change = daily chlorine × stabilizer per ppm × 7 − monthly loss × 7 ÷ 30
projection.p2: Stabilizer is not permanent, but it is stubborn. It is not destroyed by the sun directly: sunlight breaks chlorine down, and the fragments released attack the stabilizer. That accounts for {degMin} to {degMax} ppm a month depending on how exposed your pool is. This tool assumes the low end, {degUsed} ppm a month, so it warns early rather than late.
projection.p3: Do not count on that loss to save you. At the default daily demand, dichlor adds around {perMonth} ppm of stabilizer a month, which is many times faster than sunlight removes it. This is why a stabilizer problem builds up over one season and takes years to notice.
projection.p4: When your product adds no stabilizer at all, the balance goes negative and there is no date to project. The tool says your level is stable or slowly falling, which is the honest answer rather than a reassuring one.

demand.title: The daily chlorine demand
demand.p1: Everything in the projection scales with how much chlorine your pool gets through in a day. Typical summer pools use {min} to {max} ppm, driven mostly by sunlight, then heat and how many people swim. The tool starts from {def} ppm a day.
demand.p2: That is an assumption, not a measurement, and you can replace it with a real one: test free chlorine, add nothing for 24 hours, test again. The difference is your pool's actual demand, and it makes every number below it more honest.

limits.title: Assumptions and limits
limits.p1: These figures are for pools chlorinated by hand. Salt-water pools with a chlorine generator run to a different stabilizer range and are outside the scope of this tool. The projection is a straight line: it ignores the fact that a higher stabilizer level slowly reduces daily chlorine loss, which means reality is usually a little slower than the projection says.
limits.p2: Nothing here replaces testing your own water. The one measurement worth doing properly is the stabilizer: it decides every other number on this page, it changes slowly, and most people have never measured it once.

ApiDocs.title: Calculation API
ApiDocs.subtitle: The same calculations the site's tools use, callable from any client.
ApiDocs.intro: Every Pool Helper calculator is exposed as a public HTTP endpoint. Endpoints take a POST request with a JSON body and respond in JSON, require no authentication, and do not log the data you send.
ApiDocs.specIntro: This page is generated from the project's OpenAPI 3.1 specification, which in turn is derived from the validation schemas the server actually uses. You can download it and use it with any compatible tool (Swagger UI, Scalar, client generators).
ApiDocs.errorsIntro: If the request body is invalid, the response is a 400 with a descriptive error field and a details field listing each validation problem. On an unexpected failure the response is a 500.

chlorine-target.summary: Target free chlorine for a shock
chlorine-target.description: Computes the free chlorine (FC) level to aim for, taking the highest of three candidates: the SLAM target (a ratio of the CYA level, scaled by how bad the water looks), breakpoint chlorination (a multiple of combined chlorine), and a per-water-condition floor. When CYA is unknown the target is returned as a min-max range instead of a single value.
chlorine-target.responseDescription: The winning target plus each candidate that was considered, and any warnings raised (for example a CYA level high enough that dilution is advised).

chlorine-dose.description: Converts the gap between the target and current free chlorine into grams of pure available chlorine for a given water volume. Ranges propagate: an unknown current FC produces a range instead of a single figure. For a range input, max must be greater than or equal to min.
chlorine-dose.responseDescription: The FC gap to close and the corresponding mass of pure available chlorine.

product-conversion.summary: Convert pure chlorine into a real product amount
product-conversion.description: Turns a mass of pure available chlorine into how much of an actual product to add, given its concentration, and reports the side effects that product has on the water (calcium hardness, salt, pH direction). For a range input, max must be greater than or equal to min.
product-conversion.responseDescription: The amount of product to add, in the unit appropriate to its physical form, plus its side effects.

pool-volume.summary: Pool water volume from shape and dimensions
pool-volume.description: Computes water volume for a rectangular or round pool. The accepted dimensions depend on the shape: a rectangle takes length, width and depth, a circle takes diameter and depth. Use the average depth, not the maximum, or the volume will be overestimated.
pool-volume.responseDescription: The same volume expressed in liters, cubic meters and US gallons.

shock.description: Runs chlorine-target, chlorine-dose and product-conversion in a single call and returns a numeric breakdown of every intermediate step. This is what the Shock Calculator UI uses. Answering "unknown" for CYA or current chlorine is supported and turns the result into a range.
shock.responseDescription: The target, dose and product results together, plus a breakdown of every value used to reach them and any warnings. When the water needs no shock, isNoShockNeeded is true and the dose and product fields are null.

chlorine.summary: Compare the real cost of two chlorine products
chlorine.description: Compares any two chlorine products on cost per kilogram of ACTIVE chlorine, which is the only fair basis for comparison. Each of the two slots (slotA, slotB) carries its own productId, so the two sides may hold different products or the same one. Products sold by volume (unit 'l') are converted to weight using density, falling back to the product's typical density when omitted; a solid product priced by the litre is reported isValid: false rather than rejected. Zero values are accepted and simply mark that slot as incomplete rather than being an error.
chlorine.responseDescription: Per-slot metrics (gross mass, active chlorine mass, cost per active kg) and the winning slot, 'A' or 'B' (or 'DRAW'). The winner is identified by slot, not by product, so that two products of the same type can be compared. When either slot is incomplete, winner is null.

chlorine-maintenance.summary: Routine chlorine target, dose, and where your stabilizer is heading
chlorine-maintenance.description: Answers the everyday question rather than the recovery one: given CYA, what free chlorine should the pool hold, how much product gets it there, and if the product is stabilized (trichlor, dichlor) how fast cyanuric acid is accumulating. Minimum FC is max(7.5% of CYA, 2 ppm) and target FC is 11.5% of CYA, both from TroubleFreePool's published Chlorine/CYA table. The projection subtracts sunlight degradation, so with an unstabilized product it returns weeksToCeiling: null and a falling trend rather than a date. Unlike /shock, stabilized products ARE accepted here: routine dosing is exactly what this endpoint measures.
chlorine-maintenance.responseDescription: The FC target band, the dose to reach it (null when already at target), the product amount with its side effects, and the CYA projection week by week. projection is null when CYA is unknown, because projecting from the fallback range would turn a guess into a countdown.

About.title: The project
About.subtitle: A summer of vibe coding, trial and error with the pool at home.

what.title: What Pool Helper is
what.p1: Pool Helper started in the summer of 2026 as a project to learn "vibe coding": building a real application while working side by side with an AI, from design to code. The goal was twofold — learn to build software this way, and at the same time put some order into what I was learning about maintaining the pool at home.

sources.title: Where the information comes from
sources.p1: The content on this site comes from hands-on experience maintaining and recovering a pool, together with YouTube videos, research done with the help of AI, and technical articles found online (in particular TroubleFreePool and Orenda, cited on each tool's page). I'm not a pool professional — every number used in the calculators is still verified and listed with its source.

why.title: Why share it
why.p1: Anyone managing a pool for the first time runs into the same questions I had. Sharing these tools and guides is a way to make what I learned useful to someone else, and it's also a project I enjoy being able to show.

howItsBuilt.title: How it's built
howItsBuilt.p1: The site is built with Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, with the stated goal of being built the right way — calculation logic separated from the UI, modular code, and public documentation for the calculation API.

About.disclaimerCallout: Before using the calculators, read the disclaimer.

Disclaimer.title: Disclaimer
Disclaimer.subtitle: Read this before using the calculators.

purpose.title: Informational purpose
purpose.p1: All content and calculators on Pool Helper are for informational and educational purposes only. They do not replace the advice of a qualified pool professional. The formulas and thresholds used are based on public sources (cited on each tool's page) and the author's personal experience, not on professional validation.

scope.title: Scope: manually chlorinated pools
scope.p1: This site's chlorine and stabilizer (CYA) guidance is meant for pools maintained with manually dosed chlorine (tablets, granules, liquid). Saltwater pools (salt chlorine generators) need a higher CYA range (roughly 70-80 ppm) and are outside the scope of this guide — if you have a salt generator, these tools aren't for you.

safety.title: Chemical safety
safety.p1: Always follow the instructions on the label of the product you're using — they take priority over anything on this site. Never mix different chemical products together (risk of hazardous reactions, toxic fumes). Store chemicals out of reach of children and pets, in a ventilated area away from heat sources.

liability.title: No liability
liability.p1: The author accepts no responsibility for damage to people, animals, equipment or property resulting from the use of the information on this site. Use of the calculators and guides is at your own risk.

privacy.title: Privacy and data
privacy.p1: Pool Helper uses no cookies, tracks no browsing activity, and requires no account. Data entered into the calculators (volume, prices, chemical values) stays entirely in the user's browser, saved locally (localStorage), and is never sent to or shared with the author or any third party.
privacy.p2: You can verify this yourself, without having to take my word for it:
privacy.githubLinkLabel: Pool Helper's source code is public on GitHub.

affiliate.title: Affiliate links
affiliate.p1: This site may in the future include affiliate links (for example to Amazon) for products mentioned in the guides — purchasing through those links may earn the author a small commission, at no extra cost to the user. This is not active yet; when it is, it will be clearly disclosed on this page.
